tools.name: Agreement of change maps
tools.description: Where and when several maps of change dates agree (Zeit's zeit.agreement): choose two or more results with dates (LandTrendr's year of detection, CCDC, BFAST or CODED break dates...), from this series or others. A change counts by its calendar year; maps agree when their years are at most the tolerance apart. Gives the consensus year and how many maps back it: changes found by several algorithms are the ones to trust. The maps are put on the grid of the first one.

params.label: Maps of change dates
params.help: Tool results whose values are dates. The outputs are on the grid of the first one checked.

params.label: Tolerance (years)
params.help: Years two changes may be apart and still agree (0: the same year).

outputs.name: Share of the maps that agree

tools.name: BFAST
tools.description: Breaks For Additive Season and Trend (Verbesselt et al. 2010), as implemented in Zeit. Iteratively splits the series into trend and seasonal components and detects breaks in each. Needs a regular series with several observations per year and more than two years.

params.label: Min segment size
params.help: Minimum segment length, as a fraction of the valid observations.

params.label: Max trend breaks
params.help: Maximum number of breaks searched for in the trend component.

params.label: Max season breaks
params.help: Maximum number of breaks searched for in the seasonal component.

params.label: Harmonic order
params.help: Number of sine/cosine pairs in the seasonal model (capped at observations per year).

params.label: Significance level
params.help: A component is only searched for breaks when the OLS-MOSUM stability test rejects at this level.

params.label: Max iterations
params.help: Maximum trend/season re-estimation rounds (usually converges much earlier).

params.label: Min observations
params.help: Pixels with fewer valid observations are not fitted.

tools.name: BFAST Lite
tools.description: Single-pass multiple-break detection (Masiliunas et al. 2021), as implemented in Zeit. Fits one segmented trend + harmonic model and picks the number of breaks by LWZ. Faster than classic BFAST. Magnitude = the model after the break minus the model before it, on the first observation after the break.

params.label: Min segment size
params.help: Minimum segment length, as a fraction of the valid observations.

params.label: Max breaks
params.help: Maximum number of breaks searched for and reported.

params.label: Harmonic order
params.help: Number of sine/cosine pairs in the seasonal model (capped at observations per year).

params.label: Min observations
params.help: Pixels with fewer valid observations are not fitted.

tools.name: BFAST Monitor
tools.description: Near-real-time disturbance monitoring (Verbesselt et al. 2012), as implemented in Zeit. Fits a stable trend + harmonic model on the history period and flags the first date in the monitoring period where the OLS-MOSUM process leaves its boundary. History = everything before the monitoring start.

params.label: Monitoring start (year)
params.help: Decimal year where monitoring begins (e.g. 2018.5). 0 = automatic: the last 25% of the series. Clamped so the history and at least one year of monitoring fit.

params.label: MOSUM window
params.help: Moving-sum window as a fraction of the history length.

params.label: Monitoring period
params.help: Maximum monitoring length relative to the history (sets the critical boundary).

params.label: Harmonic order
params.help: Number of sine/cosine pairs in the seasonal model (capped at observations per year).

params.label: Significance level
params.help: Significance level of the monitoring boundary.

params.label: Min history obs.
params.help: Pixels with fewer valid observations in the history period are not fitted.

tools.name: BEAST (Bayesian changepoints)
tools.description: Bayesian Estimator of Abrupt change, Seasonal change and Trend (Zhao et al. 2019), as in Zeit (zeit.beast, a port of Rbeast's C code, the same results from the same seed): the series is decomposed into a piecewise trend and a piecewise harmonic season whose changepoints, how many and where, are sampled by MCMC and averaged over all the models instead of one chosen. What comes out is the probability of a change at each date, the most probable changepoints with their probability and jump, and the trend with its 95% interval: an alternative to BFAST that says how sure each break is, robust to noise and gaps. Irregular dates are averaged onto a regular grid first. Every pixel is its own MCMC: a whole image is slow; try the visible area, an ROI or fewer samples first.

params.label: Season
labels: Automatic (harmonic with 4 or more dates a year)
params.help: A harmonic season of a year fitted with the trend, and its own changepoints; none for annual series.

params.label: Grid step (years)
params.help: The step of the regular grid the dates are averaged onto, in years: 1/12 monthly, 1/23 16-day, 1 annual. 0 = chosen from the dates as Rbeast does (a day, half a month, a month or a week).

params.label: Max trend changepoints
params.help: The most changepoints the trend may have (Rbeast's tcp.minmax).

params.label: Max season changepoints
params.help: The most changepoints the season may have (scp.minmax).

params.label: Max trend order
params.help: The highest polynomial degree of a trend segment: 1 linear, 0 flat.

params.label: MCMC samples
params.help: Samples kept per chain (Rbeast's default 8000): more are steadier and slower; a pixel takes about 4 ms per 1000 samples and chain on an annual series of 40 years, some 40 ms on a 16-day series of 25 years.

params.label: Chains
params.help: Independent MCMC chains, averaged (Rbeast's default 3).

params.label: Burn-in
params.help: Samples discarded at the start of each chain.

params.label: Thinning
params.help: One sample kept every this many.

params.label: Seed
params.help: The random seed: the same seed gives the same result (Rbeast's too).

tools.name: CCDC
tools.description: Continuous Change Detection and Classification (Zhu & Woodcock 2014), Zeit's port of the original MATLAB code. Fits harmonic models to every band of a surface-reflectance series (Landsat-style: blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, optional thermal) with a quality band, and starts a new model when consecutive clear observations depart from the current one. Needs several bands per date (map them to the roles below) and real dates; a quality band (Fmask or Landsat QA_PIXEL) is strongly recommended. Break magnitude = jump between the segment models at the break over the detection bands (reflectance x 10000).

params.label: Reflectance units
params.help: CCDC's thresholds are defined on reflectance x 10000. Automatic: median <= 2 -> reflectance 0-1; median >= 6500 -> Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 digital numbers (x 0.0000275 - 0.2); otherwise already x 10000. Janus applies the files' scale/offset metadata first, when present.

params.label: Consecutive anomalies
params.help: Consecutive anomalous clear observations needed to flag a change (the original's 'conse').

params.label: Change probability
params.help: Chi-square probability of the change threshold over the detection bands.

params.label: Outlier probability
params.help: Chi-square probability above which a single observation is an outlier, not change.

params.label: Max coefficients
params.help: Maximum number of harmonic model coefficients per band.

params.label: Max segments
params.help: Segments kept per pixel.

tools.name: CCDC synthetic image
tools.description: The image CCDC's harmonic models predict for one date (zeit.predict_synthetic_image): every band, in the series' units, and the quantity the series shows (e.g. NDVI), free of clouds, gaps and noise. Each pixel uses the segment that covers the date (before the first, the first; after the last, the last). Runs CCDC first, with the parameters below.

params.label: Date
params.help: Decimal year to predict (e.g. 2019.5 = early July 2019); 0: the date shown on the map.

params.label: Reflectance units
params.help: CCDC's thresholds are defined on reflectance x 10000. Automatic: median <= 2 -> reflectance 0-1; median >= 6500 -> Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 digital numbers (x 0.0000275 - 0.2); otherwise already x 10000. Janus applies the files' scale/offset metadata first, when present.

params.label: Consecutive anomalies
params.help: Consecutive anomalous clear observations needed to flag a change (the original's 'conse').

params.label: Change probability
params.help: Chi-square probability of the change threshold over the detection bands.

params.label: Outlier probability
params.help: Chi-square probability above which a single observation is an outlier, not change.

params.label: Max coefficients
params.help: Maximum number of harmonic model coefficients per band.

params.label: Max segments
params.help: Segments kept per pixel.

tools.name: S-CCD (stochastic CCDC)
tools.description: Stochastic Continuous Change Detection (Ye et al. 2021), as in Zeit (zeit.sccd): CCDC's harmonic models of every band (trend, annual and semiannual cycles), started on the first stable observations as CCDC's and then carried forward by a Kalman filter instead of refitted, so they follow slow changes and a new image costs one update. A change is several consecutive clear observations departing from the model over the detection bands (green to SWIR2); at the end of the series, the latest anomalous observations are a change in progress, not yet confirmed: the near-real-time state for monitoring. Needs the six Landsat-style reflectance bands mapped and real dates; a quality band (Fmask or Landsat QA_PIXEL) is strongly recommended. Faster than CCDC on long series.

params.label: Reflectance units
params.help: S-CCD's valid range and magnitudes are defined on reflectance x 10000. Automatic: median <= 2 -> reflectance 0-1; median >= 6500 -> Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 digital numbers (x 0.0000275 - 0.2); otherwise already x 10000. Janus applies the files' scale/offset metadata first, when present.

params.label: Consecutive anomalies
params.help: Consecutive anomalous clear observations that make a change (the peek window).

params.label: Change probability
params.help: Chi-square probability of the change threshold over the detection bands.

params.label: Outlier probability
params.help: Chi-square probability above which a single observation is an outlier, left out of the model.

params.label: Max angle (degrees)
params.help: Largest mean angle of the anomalous observations' change vectors to their median: a change departs in a consistent direction, noise does not.

params.label: Max segments
params.help: Segments kept per pixel.

outputs.name: Monitoring state (last date)
classes: Waiting for a model after a change

tools.name: CODED (degradation)
tools.description: Continuous Degradation Detection (Bullock et al. 2020), as implemented in Zeit: the NDFI of every observation (spectral unmixing, Souza et al. 2005) is modelled over a training period, and observations falling well below the model afterwards are a change. A change after which the land is still forest is degradation (selective logging, understory fire); otherwise it is deforestation. Needs Landsat-style surface reflectance (blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2) with real dates; a quality band is strongly recommended.

params.label: Reflectance units
params.help: The unmixing endmembers are reflectances. Automatic: median <= 2 -> reflectance 0-1; median >= 6500 -> Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 digital numbers (x 0.0000275 - 0.2); otherwise already x 10000. Janus applies the files' scale/offset metadata first, when present.

params.label: Monitoring start (year)
params.help: Year the monitoring starts; the training period is the years before it. 0 = the training period starts with the series.

params.label: Training period (years)
params.help: Years of the training period, whose NDFI model the monitoring compares with.

params.label: Consecutive observations
params.help: Observations in a row beyond the threshold that make a change.

params.label: Threshold (RMSEs)
params.help: How far below the model, in RMSEs of the training fit, an observation must fall.

params.label: Years after a change
params.help: Years modelled as the land cover after a change, and the least time between two changes.

params.label: Min observations
params.help: Least observations to fit a model (training, or after a change).

params.label: Changes
params.help: Only drops of the NDFI (disturbances, as CODED), or rises too.

params.label: Max changes
params.help: Changes kept per pixel.

params.label: Forest NDFI
params.help: Forest where a model's mean NDFI is at least this (before: forest or not; after a change: degradation or deforestation). Closed forest is near 1; open woodlands are naturally lower.

params.label: Max cloud fraction
params.help: Observations whose unmixed cloud fraction is above this are left out (CODED: 0.05); 1 keeps them all.

outputs.name: NDFI change at the first change
Mean NDFI of the training period

tools.name: LandTrendr
tools.description: Temporal segmentation of annual series (Kennedy et al. 2010), as implemented in Zeit. Fits a sequence of straight segments and maps the greatest (or newest, fastest...) loss or gain event per pixel.

params.label: Event
params.help: Direction of change of interest. Orients the segmentation (Zeit's direction) and selects which segments become events.

params.label: Max segments
params.help: Maximum number of segments in the fitted trajectory.

params.label: p-value threshold
params.help: Models with a worse p-value are rejected.

params.label: Recovery threshold
params.help: Maximum recovery rate per year (1/years).

params.label: Spike threshold
params.help: Desawtooth dampening of single-year spikes (1 = none).

params.label: Best model proportion
params.help: Prefer the model with most vertices whose p-value is within (2 - this) times the best one.

params.label: Vertex count overshoot
params.help: Extra candidate vertices before pruning.

params.label: Min observations
params.help: Pixels with fewer valid years are not fitted.

params.label: Pick event by
params.help: Which event is mapped when a pixel has several (raster runs).

params.label: Min magnitude
params.help: Events smaller than this are ignored (raster runs).

params.label: Min duration (years)
params.help: Events shorter than this are ignored (raster runs).

params.label: Pre-event value threshold
params.help: Loss: ignore events starting below this value. Gain: ignore events starting above it. 0 = off.

tools.name: Mann-Kendall trend
tools.description: Mann-Kendall monotonic trend test with Sen's slope, ported from pymannkendall to C++ in Zeit. Hamed-Rao and Yue-Wang correct the variance for serial correlation (usual in EO composites); the seasonal variant (Hirsch & Slack) tests sub-annual series per season. The first map shows Sen's slope only where the trend is significant.

params.label: Method
params.help: Hamed-Rao is the usual choice for annual EO composites, which are serially correlated. Seasonal pools per-season tests for sub-annual series.

params.label: Significance level
params.help: A trend is significant when its p-value is below this.

params.label: Autocorrelation lags
params.help: Hamed-Rao / Yue-Wang only: number of first lags used by the correction (-1 = all).

params.label: Seasons per year
params.help: Seasonal method only: observations per cycle (12 monthly, 23 MODIS 16-day). 0 = automatic, from the dates.

params.label: Min valid observations
params.help: Pixels with fewer valid observations are left empty (raster runs).

tools.name: NDFI (spectral unmixing)
tools.description: Spectral mixture analysis (Zeit's zeit.unmix) of every observation into green vegetation, non-photosynthetic vegetation, soil, shade and cloud fractions, with the endmembers of Souza et al. (2005), and their NDFI: near 1 in closed forest, lower where logging or fire opened the canopy, below 0 on soil and pasture. Needs Landsat-style surface reflectance (blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2) with real dates. A raster run writes the NDFI as a series and opens it as a new layer, ready for LandTrendr, BFAST and the other tools.

params.label: Reflectance units
params.help: The endmembers are reflectances. Automatic: median <= 2 -> reflectance 0-1; median >= 6500 -> Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 digital numbers (x 0.0000275 - 0.2); otherwise already x 10000. Janus applies the files' scale/offset metadata first, when present.

params.label: Max cloud fraction
params.help: Observations whose cloud fraction is above this are left out (CODED: 0.05); 1 keeps every observation. The quality band, when set, is applied first.

params.label: Also write the fractions
params.help: Raster runs: also write the GV, NPV, soil and shade fractions, each as a series (opened as layers).

tools.name: Phenology
tools.description: Land surface phenology as implemented in Zeit (written from the papers, with the methods of phenofit): smooths the series, splits it into growing seasons, fits a curve to each season and derives its start (SOS), peak (POS) and end (EOS). Needs a sub-annual vegetation index series (e.g. NDVI/EVI, 8-16 day or monthly). Maps summarize the seasons per pixel (median, latest or a given year); dates are days of the year of the season's peak.

params.label: Curve
params.help: Function fitted to each season.

params.label: Season start/end
params.help: How SOS and EOS are read from the fitted curve. POS is always the curve's maximum.

params.label: Smoothing
params.help: Smoothing used to find the seasons (the curves are fitted to the observations).

params.label: Whittaker lambda
params.help: Whittaker only: larger = smoother.

params.label: HANTS frequencies
params.help: HANTS only: number of harmonics per year.

params.label: Min pixel amplitude
params.help: Pixels whose series varies less than this (water, urban, bare soil) are skipped. Use the index scale (e.g. 0.1 for NDVI, 1000 for NDVI x 10000).

params.label: Min season amplitude
params.help: Seasons with a smaller rise above their troughs are dropped.

params.label: Min season length (days)
params.help: Seasons shorter than this (trough to trough) are dropped.

params.label: Season mapped
labels: Season peaking in the year below
params.help: Raster runs: how the seasons of each pixel become one map.

params.label: Year
params.help: With 'Season peaking in the year below': calendar year of the peak (0 = latest).

tools.name: Smoothing
tools.description: Smoothed curve of the series on the chart, with Zeit's Whittaker smoother (penalises roughness, follows the real spacing of the dates and fills gaps with the curve) or Savitzky-Golay filter (local polynomial over evenly spaced dates; gaps are interpolated first).

params.label: Method
params.help: Whittaker handles gaps and uneven dates and is a common choice for vegetation indices.

params.label: Whittaker lambda
params.help: Larger = smoother (10 is light for a 16-day series, 1000 strong). Its meaning does not depend on the spacing of the dates.

params.label: S-G window (dates)
params.help: Odd number of observations in each local fit (made odd and capped at the series length).

params.label: S-G polynomial order
params.help: Order of the local polynomial (below the window length).

tools.name: SOM clustering
tools.description: Self-Organizing Map (Kohonen), as implemented in Zeit: unsupervised clustering of the pixels by their whole series. The map is trained on a sample of the area, then every pixel goes to the nearest neuron; neighbouring neurons hold similar series. The result is a cluster map; hover it to see the typical series of the cluster under the cursor on the chart. Good for a first look at what kinds of trajectories an area has.

params.label: Grid columns
params.help: Neurons per row of the map: columns x rows clusters (at most 12).

params.label: Grid rows
params.help: Rows of neurons of the map: columns x rows clusters (at most 12).

params.label: Training sample (pixels)
params.help: Pixels the map is trained on, drawn at random from rows spread over the area.

params.label: Training passes
params.help: Passes over the sample (online training: one update per pixel and pass).

params.label: Dates without a value
params.help: A pixel needs a value on every date: fill the gaps linearly between its neighbours in time (the first and last values repeat at the ends), or leave such pixels without a cluster.

params.label: Min dates with a value (%)
params.help: When interpolating: pixels with values on fewer dates get no cluster.

params.label: Random seed
params.help: Seed of the sample and of the training (same seed, same clusters).

tools.name: k-means clustering
tools.description: k-means (Lloyd's, started by k-means++ as scikit-learn's KMeans, the best of several starts): unsupervised clustering of the pixels by their whole series. The centres are fitted on a sample of the area, then every pixel goes to the nearest one; the clusters are ordered by their centres' mean value, low to high. Run from the Classification window with samples, each cluster is named by the class of most of the samples in it. The result is a cluster map; hover it to see the typical series (the centre) of the cluster under the cursor on the chart.

params.label: Clusters
params.help: Number of clusters (at most 12).

params.label: Training sample (pixels)
params.help: Pixels the centres are fitted on, drawn at random from rows spread over the area.

params.label: Starts
params.help: k-means runs from different k-means++ starts; the one whose pixels are nearest their centres (least inertia) is kept, as scikit-learn's n_init.

params.label: Dates without a value
params.help: A pixel needs a value on every date: fill the gaps linearly between its neighbours in time (the first and last values repeat at the ends), or leave such pixels without a cluster.

params.label: Min dates with a value (%)
params.help: When interpolating: pixels with values on fewer dates get no cluster.

params.label: Random seed
params.help: Seed of the sample and of the starts (same seed, same clusters).

tools.name: Tmask (cloud screening)
tools.description: Tmask (Zhu & Woodcock 2014), as implemented in Zeit: a robust harmonic model of each pixel's green and SWIR1 series flags the observations that are too bright in green (clouds) or too dark in SWIR (shadows) for their date, which a quality band often misses (haze, thin clouds, shadow edges). Needs the green and SWIR1 bands and real dates. A raster run writes the series shown without the flagged observations and opens it as a new layer. The model spans the whole series: after a sudden lasting change (a clearing) the observations can look like clouds to it, so check such pixels on the chart.

params.label: Reflectance units
params.help: Tmask's thresholds are in reflectance (0.04). Automatic: median <= 2 -> reflectance 0-1; median >= 6500 -> Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 digital numbers (x 0.0000275 - 0.2); otherwise already x 10000. Janus applies the files' scale/offset metadata first, when present.

params.label: Write the screened series
params.help: Raster runs: also write the series shown without the flagged observations (opened as a new layer).

tools.name: TWDTW classification
tools.description: Time-Weighted Dynamic Time Warping (Maus et al. 2016), as implemented in Zeit (the distance of the R package twdtw). Each pixel gets the class of the most similar pattern: drop pins on places you know (forest, crop, pasture...), add them below as classes and name them. A pattern may match any stretch of the series; matching dates far apart in time is penalised by the time weight.

params.label: Classes
params.help: One reference series per class, taken from a pin or the ROI mean. Drop a pin on a place whose class you know, choose it in the list and give the class a name. Several patterns may share a name (they are separate entries in the legend).

params.label: Time weight: steepness
params.help: Slope of the logistic time weight, per day (larger = sharper transition at the midpoint).

params.label: Time weight: midpoint (days)
params.help: Time apart, in days, at which matching two dates costs half a unit more than matching the same date.

params.label: Time measured
params.help: Between the dates: for patterns that cover the period of the series (a pin's whole series). Between days of the year (31 December and 1 January are a day apart): for patterns of one season, which then match that season in any year.

params.label: Max time apart (days)
params.help: Dates more than this apart are never matched. 0 = no limit. The time weight adds at most 1 per pair of dates: on series with large values (e.g. reflectance x 10000) only this limit keeps a pattern near its own dates.

params.label: Max distance
params.help: Pixels whose best distance is above this stay unclassified. 0 = classify every pixel.

params.label: Min valid observations
params.help: Pixels with fewer valid dates stay unclassified.

tools.name: Post-processing (classes)
tools.description: Cleans a classification, a categorical layer of one map or a map per date (a land cover series, a model's class map), as Zeit's post-processing: the short excursions of each pixel's classes removed first (forest, pasture, forest becomes forest three times: zeit.desawtooth_classes), then each date's map through a majority filter (zeit.apply_majority_filter) and a minimum mapping unit that merges the patches under a size into the neighbouring class with which they share the longest border (zeit.mmu_sieve, as GDAL's sieve: the map stays complete). A raster run writes the cleaned classes, opened as a new layer with the layer's class names and colours, and how many dates of each pixel changed. On the chart: the pixel's classes after the temporal filter (the spatial filters need the neighbours: raster runs).

params.label: Temporal: longest excursion (dates)
params.help: A run of up to this many dates of one class between two runs of another, the same before and after (A B A), takes that class (A A A). 0: off. Needs 3 dates or more.

params.label: Majority window
params.help: Each pixel takes the most common class of this window (odd: 3 = 3 x 3), its own on a tie. 0: off.

params.label: Majority iterations
params.help: How many times the majority filter runs (it stops early when nothing changes).

params.label: Minimum mapping unit
params.help: Patches of fewer pixels are merged, the smallest first, into the neighbouring patch of the longest shared border, taking its class (11 Landsat pixels are about 1 ha). 0: off.

params.label: Patches
params.help: Whether pixels touching by a corner belong to one patch.

tools.name: SNIC segmentation
tools.description: SNIC superpixels (Achanta & Süsstrunk 2017), as zeit.snic: the area divided into segments of pixels whose whole series are alike (each date, or each band of each date, is one value compared), grown from seeds on R snic's grids, as sits_segment does. A raster run writes the segments' labels, each segment's mean series (opened as a new layer) and the segments' polygons in a GeoPackage (opened as a vector layer), with their size, centre and mean of every value: ready to interpret by object, to extract series from, or to classify one sample a segment.

params.label: Values compared
labels: The shown band or index of every date
params.help: Shown: the series shown on the map (the band, or the normalized difference, with the quality band applied). Every band: all the bands of every date, so pixels are alike when all their bands are (more memory and time).

params.label: Seed spacing
params.help: Distance between the seeds, in pixels (sits_segment's default: 10): about the side of a segment.

params.label: Seed grid
params.help: R snic's grids: rectangular; diamond (a second grid shifted by half a step, the step scaled by 1.41); hexagonal (the column step scaled by 1.73); random (as many seeds as the rectangular grid, drawn at random).

params.label: Compactness
params.help: Larger: more regular, compact segments; smaller: segments follow the data more closely. The values' differences are in their own units: 0.5 (sits' default) for reflectance or an index in 0-1, about 5000 for reflectance x 10000.

params.label: Margin
params.help: The margin along the edges kept free of seeds, in seed spacings (0.5: half a spacing, R snic's default).

params.label: Tile size
params.help: The area is segmented in tiles of this many pixels a side, in parallel; segments never cross the tiles' edges. 0: the whole area at once (one core, and the whole area in memory).

params.label: Dates without a value
params.help: A pixel is compared on every date: fill the gaps linearly between its neighbours in time (the first and last values repeat at the ends), or leave such pixels out of every segment.

params.label: Min dates with a value (%)
params.help: When interpolating: pixels with values on fewer dates are left out of every segment.

params.label: Random seed
params.help: Seed of the random grid (same seed, same seeds).

params.label: Write the polygons
params.help: Also write the segments as polygons in a GeoPackage, with their size, centre and mean of every value compared (a column each, up to 1000), and open them as a vector layer.

tools.name: Texture (GLCM)
tools.description: The texture of the series in a moving window, as zeit.texture: the grey-level co-occurrence matrix's properties (Haralick et al. 1973, as scikit-image's graycomatrix and graycoprops give them, averaged over four directions) and three window statistics of spfeas (the mean, the standard deviation and the mean Sobel gradient), of a temporal summary of the shown series (its median, maximum, amplitude...). Fields, pastures, orchards, plantations and forests differ in texture where their spectra are alike: the maps are inputs for a classifier, and show the grain of a landscape. A raster run writes one map per feature. The windows need their neighbours: raster runs only.

params.label: Summary of the dates
params.help: The image whose texture is measured: each pixel's summary of the shown series over the dates (with a single date, that date).

params.label: Window
params.help: The window's side in pixels (odd; an even one is made odd): the scale of the texture. 5-9 for fields at 10 m.

params.label: Grey levels
params.help: The values are quantized to this many levels between their 2nd and 98th percentiles before the co-occurrences are counted (scikit-image's levels). Fewer: smoother, faster.

params.label: Pair distance
params.help: How far apart the pixels of a pair are (in each of the four directions).

params.label: GLCM properties
params.help: Contrast, dissimilarity, homogeneity, angular second moment, energy, correlation, entropy, and the GLCM's mean and variance.

params.label: Window statistics
params.help: The window's mean, standard deviation and mean gradient magnitude (spfeas's simplest features).

tools.name: AR(1) trend (remotePARTS)
tools.description: Linear trend with AR(1) errors fitted by REML (remotePARTS's fitAR, Ives et al. 2021), in Zeit: a t-test of the trend that accounts for the autocorrelation of the series, a parametric alternative to Mann-Kendall. The first map shows the slope only where it is significant. Analysis > Trend test (PARTS) tests these trends over a region, accounting for the spatial correlation of the pixels.

params.label: Trend per
params.help: The unit of the slope: per year of the dates, or per observation as remotePARTS's default.

params.label: Harmonics
params.help: Pairs of harmonics (cos, sin) of the yearly cycle fitted with the trend, for sub-annual series (0 for annual composites).

params.label: Missing dates
params.help: Exact: observations k dates apart are correlated by rho^k. Ignored: the valid observations are taken as consecutive.

params.label: Significance level
params.help: A trend is significant when its p-value is below this.

params.label: Min valid observations
params.help: Pixels with fewer valid observations are left empty (at least the model's terms + 2).

tools.name: Recovery (LandTrendr)
tools.description: How each pixel recovered after its disturbance, as in Zeit (zeit.recovery_metrics): LandTrendr segments the annual series, the greatest (or newest...) loss is the disturbance, and its fitted trajectory after the trough gives the years to recovery (Y2R), R80P, the relative recovery indicator (RRI), the absolute recovery (ARI) and the year-on-year recovery (YrYr) (Kennedy et al. 2012; White et al. 2017; Frazier et al. 2018).

params.label: Event
labels: Loss (the index drops with the disturbance)
params.help: Direction of the disturbance: loss for indices that drop (NBR, NDVI, TCW), gain for those that rise (SWIR bands). Gains need the recovery level 'Fraction of the loss'.

params.label: Max segments
params.help: Maximum number of segments in the fitted trajectory.

params.label: p-value threshold
params.help: Models with a worse p-value are rejected.

params.label: Recovery threshold
params.help: Maximum recovery rate per year (1/years).

params.label: Spike threshold
params.help: Desawtooth dampening of single-year spikes (1 = none).

params.label: Best model proportion
params.help: Prefer the model with most vertices whose p-value is within (2 - this) times the best one.

params.label: Vertex count overshoot
params.help: Extra candidate vertices before pruning.

params.label: Min observations
params.help: Pixels with fewer valid years are not fitted.

params.label: Pick event by
params.help: Which disturbance is measured when a pixel has several.

params.label: Min magnitude
params.help: Events smaller than this are ignored.

params.label: Min duration (years)
params.help: Events shorter than this are ignored.

params.label: Pre-event value threshold
params.help: Loss: ignore events starting below this value. Gain: ignore events starting above it. 0 = off.

params.label: Horizon (years)
params.help: Years after the trough at which the recovery is measured (ARI, RRI, R80P, YrYr): the best of the fitted values of years horizon - 1 and horizon (Frazier et al. 2018).

params.label: Recovered at (fraction)
params.help: The fraction of the pre-disturbance value (or of the loss) a pixel must return to: 0.8 for the 80% of White et al. (2017)'s Y2R and R80P.

params.label: Recovery level
params.help: Pre-disturbance value: recovered at target x the value before (White et al. 2017; an index that is positive and drops, such as NBR). Loss regained: recovered once that fraction of the drop came back (any index, either direction).

params.label: Pre-disturbance years
params.help: Years averaged for the pre-disturbance value, up to the disturbance's start.

tools.name: EWMACD (monitoring)
tools.description: Continuous monitoring of every observation (irregular, cloudy dates welcome) with EWMA control charts, as in Zeit (zeit.ewmacd; Brooks et al. 2014): a harmonic model of the training years, refitted without the clouds an X-bar chart screens; the residuals of every date after them smoothed by an EWMA, which signals when it stays beyond its control limits: a disturbance below, a gain above. Subtle shifts (thinning, drought, pests) as well as clearcuts; the date the pixel came back within its limits is its recovery. The flags are those of Brooks' EWMACD script (the paper's, Earth Engine's Ewmacd).

params.label: Training ends before (year)
params.help: The first year after the training period: the model is fitted on the years before it and the monitoring starts with it. 0 = three years of training (Brooks' default). The training years should be stable: a pixel disturbed in them signals as soon as they end.

params.label: EWMA weight (lambda)
params.help: Weight of each new observation in the moving average: low values are slow and smooth (subtle changes, few false signals), 1 a chart of each date alone (Brooks et al.: 0.3; 0.1-0.5 comparable).

params.label: Control limits (sigmas)
params.help: The control limits in standard deviations of the EWMA; the flags count how many limits the EWMA is beyond.

params.label: Persistence (dates)
params.help: Consecutive dates a signal must last to count (Earth Engine's default 3); a shorter run keeps the state before it.

params.label: Harmonic order
params.help: Sine/cosine pairs of the seasonal model of the training years (Brooks et al.: 2).

params.label: Training screen (sigmas)
params.help: Training dates farther than this from the model (clouds, shadows) are left out of the fit and of the chart (an X-bar chart).

params.label: Monitoring screen (sigmas)
params.help: Later dates farther than this from the model are left out as gross anomalies; the changes must stay in. A clearcut larger than this on a smooth series is screened until it comes back within it: raise it for such series.

tools.name: Spectral unmixing (endmembers)
tools.description: Linear spectral mixture analysis with endmembers of the image, as in Zeit (zeit.unmix with a table of endmembers): the fraction of each endmember (vegetation, soil, water, shade...) in every pixel and date, from all the bands of each date, and the RMSE of the rebuilt spectrum (Adams et al. 1995). The endmembers are the bands of pins at the map's date. Observations the chart leaves out (no data, the quality band's mask) are left out. A raster run writes each fraction as a series, opened as a new layer for LandTrendr, BFAST and the other tools, and their means as maps.

params.label: Endmembers
params.help: The pure spectra the pixels are mixtures of: the bands of a pin at the map's date. Drop pins on places of a known, pure cover (dense vegetation, bare soil, water, shade...), add each here and name it. Two to six usually; at most one fewer than the bands without the sum-to-one constraint. Bands without a value in one of them (the quality band, a scene's empty bands) are left out.

params.label: Constraints
params.help: Fully constrained least squares (Heinz & Chang 2001) gives fractions from 0 to 1 that add up to one; without the constraints the fractions can be negative or above one where the endmembers do not describe the pixel (the RMSE shows where).

tools.name: Spectral unmixing (spectrum)
tools.description: Linear spectral mixture analysis of a scene of one band per wavelength (hyperspectral: EnMAP, PRISMA, EMIT, AVIRIS...), as in Zeit (zeit.unmix): the fraction of each endmember in every pixel and the RMSE of the rebuilt spectrum. The endmembers are the spectra of pins. The chart draws the spectrum the fractions rebuild and each endmember's part of it.

params.label: Endmembers
params.help: The pure spectra the pixels are mixtures of: the spectra of pins. Drop pins on places of a known, pure cover (dense vegetation, bare soil, water, shade...), add each here and name it. Two to six usually; at most one fewer than the bands without the sum-to-one constraint. Bands without a value in one of them (the quality band, a scene's empty bands) are left out.

params.label: Constraints
params.help: Fully constrained least squares (Heinz & Chang 2001) gives fractions from 0 to 1 that add up to one; without the constraints the fractions can be negative or above one where the endmembers do not describe the pixel (the RMSE shows where).

tools.name: Emerging hot spots
tools.description: Emerging hot spot analysis (ESRI's Space Time Pattern Mining; sfdep's emerging_hotspot_analysis), as zeit.emerging_hotspots: at every date the Getis-Ord Gi* z-score of each pixel (its neighbourhood within a radius, at that date and the dates before it, against the date's mean), a hot spot where it is significantly high, a cold spot where significantly low; then the Mann-Kendall trend of each pixel's Gi* and its pattern as ESRI defines them: new, consecutive, intensifying, persistent, diminishing, sporadic, oscillating or historical hot or cold spot. Where the values (losses, an anomaly, a count) concentrate and how that changed. A raster run writes the patterns (a categorical map), the Gi* of every date (opened as a new layer: hover it for a pixel's Gi* series), its trend and how many dates each pixel was a hot or cold spot. The neighbourhoods need the whole map: raster runs only.

params.label: Radius
params.help: The neighbourhood: the pixels within this distance, the pixel among them (1 and a square: the 8 neighbours, queen contiguity, sfdep's default). Wider finds wider clusters.

params.label: Neighbourhood
params.help: Square: (2 radius + 1) x (2 radius + 1) pixels. Circle: those whose centres are within the radius.

params.label: Dates before
params.help: The dates before each date also in its neighbourhood (sfdep's k, ESRI's neighbourhood time step): 1 smooths each Gi* with the date before.

params.label: Against
params.help: Each date's mean and deviation (as sfdep: a place hot against the others at that date), or those of every date together (a date high everywhere is hot everywhere).

params.label: Significance level
params.help: A Gi* is a hot or cold spot when its two-sided p-value is below this; the same level for its trend.

params.label: Trend test
params.help: The test of each pixel's Gi* series (intensifying, diminishing or persistent). The Gi* of consecutive dates share neighbours, so their series are autocorrelated: Hamed-Rao corrects for it.

tools.name: Interpolate (regular grid)
tools.description: Interpolates each pixel's series to a regular grid of dates: FORCE's TSA interpolation (Frantz 2019), as zeit.interpolate. The grid starts at the first date of the series and has a date every step days (16 by default, FORCE's) up to the last one. The methods: radial basis functions (an ensemble of Gaussian kernels of several widths, each weighted by the data it finds around each date), linear interpolation between the valid observations on either side, the moving average of the valid observations within a window of days, and a harmonic model (a robust fit of an offset, a trend and up to three harmonics, predicted at every date). Missing observations (clouds, the quality band, NoData) are ignored; a date with no data within reach is empty. A raster run writes one band per date of the new grid, with its date as the band description, and opens it as a series of its own. The series needs real dates.

params.label: Method
params.help: Radial basis functions (FORCE's default) smooth the gaps and the noise with several kernel widths at once; linear keeps every valid observation; the moving average and the harmonic model smooth more.

params.label: Step
params.help: Days between the dates of the new grid (FORCE's default is 16). It starts at the first date of the series; the last date is the last one that fits before the end of the series.

params.label: Kernel widths
params.help: Radial basis functions only: the standard deviations of the Gaussian kernels, in days. Narrow kernels follow the data closely; wide ones reach across long gaps.

params.label: Kernel mass kept
params.help: Radial basis functions only: each kernel is cut where the share of its mass kept reaches this value.

params.label: Window
params.help: Moving average only: the half-width, in days. The mean of the valid observations within this many days of each date of the grid (closed: |t - date| <= window).

params.label: Harmonics
params.help: Harmonic model only: the number of harmonics of the year (1 to 3).

params.label: Trend
params.help: Harmonic model only: add a linear trend to the offset.

tools.name: Temporal metrics (FORCE STM)
tools.description: Statistics of each pixel's series over all of it: FORCE's spatio-temporal metrics (STM, Frantz 2019), as zeit.temporal_metrics. Choose the metrics (minimum, percentiles, median, maximum, range, interquartile range, mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis, number of observations); a raster run writes one map per metric, a pixel run lists their values. Missing observations (clouds, the quality band, NoData) are ignored; a pixel without a valid observation is empty (0 for the count).

params.label: Metrics
params.help: The statistics of the valid observations of each pixel: percentiles as numpy's (linear interpolation), the standard deviation of the sample (n - 1, as FORCE), skewness and excess kurtosis from the population moments (undefined, NaN, for a series with fewer than 2 distinct values), and the number of observations (0 where there is none). One map per metric.

tools.name: Fold by period (FORCE)
tools.description: The same statistics by period of the year instead of over the whole series: FORCE's fold (Frantz 2019), as zeit.temporal_metrics with a period. By year (each year from the first date's to the last's, so a year without data is an empty band), quarter, month, week or day of the year (the quarters, months, weeks and days of every year together; the calendar has 365 days, 29 February sharing day 60 with 1 March, and the week is the day's number over 7, rounded up, at most 52). A raster run writes, for each metric, one band per period named after it (a yearly series opens as dated; the others as named bands); a pixel run draws the yearly values and lists the others. The series needs real dates. Missing observations (clouds, the quality band, NoData) are ignored; a pixel without a valid observation is empty (0 for the count).

params.label: Metrics
params.help: The statistics of the valid observations of each pixel: percentiles as numpy's (linear interpolation), the standard deviation of the sample (n - 1, as FORCE), skewness and excess kurtosis from the population moments (undefined, NaN, for a series with fewer than 2 distinct values), and the number of observations (0 where there is none). One map per metric.

params.label: Period
labels: Day of the year (of every year)
params.help: The periods the statistics are taken over: every year, or the same quarter, month, week or day of the year across all the years.

tools.name: Standardize (FORCE)
tools.description: Standardizes each pixel's series along time: FORCE's STANDARDIZE, as zeit.standardize. The mean (and, for the z-score, the sample standard deviation) are those of the valid observations; missing observations stay empty, a series with fewer than 2 valid observations is left as it is, and a constant series gives empty values when normalized. A raster run writes the standardized series on the run's dates.

params.label: Method
labels: z-score (minus the mean, over the standard deviation)
params.help: The z-score puts every series on the same scale (mean 0, standard deviation 1); centring only removes the mean.

tools.name: Linear trend of a fold (FORCE)
tools.description: FORCE's trend analysis (TSA trend: TRY, TRQ, TRM, TRW, TRD), as zeit.linear_trend over zeit.temporal_metrics with a period: a statistic of each pixel's series is taken by period (each year, or each quarter, month, week or day of the year across the years; see Fold by period), then a least-squares line is fit to it, x being the position of the period (0, 1, 2...: the slope is per period, per year when folded by year; periods without a value count as steps but are skipped by the fit), with a t-test of the slope. A pixel with fewer than 3 periods with a value is empty. A raster run writes one map per chosen statistic of the fit; a pixel run draws the folded values and the line (by year) and lists the statistics. The series needs real dates.

params.label: Statistic of each period
params.help: The statistic taken over the observations of each period (the fold the trend is fit to); the mean is FORCE's usual choice.

params.label: Period
labels: Day of the year (of every year)
params.help: The periods the statistic is folded into, and so the steps of the trend: every year (the slope is per year), or the same quarter, month, week or day of the year across all the years (the slope is per quarter, month...). Periods without a value are skipped by the fit but still count as steps.

params.label: Confidence level
params.help: Confidence level of the t-test of the slope (0.95: significance level 0.05).

params.label: Test
labels: Decrease only (is the slope significantly negative?)
Increase only (is the slope significantly positive?)
params.help: The tail of the test of the slope: with one tail only a slope on that side can be significant (the significance is -1 for a decrease, 1 for an increase, 0 otherwise).

params.label: Statistics
params.help: The statistics of the fit to write, a map each. The offset is the fit at the first period, the gain the slope times the number of periods (as a percentage of the offset, 0 unless the offset is positive), R² is 0-1, the significance -1, 0 or 1, the errors those of the fit's residuals.

tools.name: Change, aftereffect, trend (FORCE CAT)
tools.description: FORCE's CAT (change, aftereffect, trend), as zeit.cat over zeit.temporal_metrics with a period: a statistic of each pixel's series is taken by period (see Fold by period), the greatest loss between a period with a value and the one with a value before it is the change, and the linear trend (as Linear trend of a fold) is fit to the whole fold, to the periods before the change (up to two before it, as FORCE defines it) and from the change on. A raster run writes one map per chosen statistic; a pixel run draws the folded values, the lines before and after the change and the change (by year), and lists the statistics. A pixel with fewer than 2 periods with a value is empty. The series needs real dates.

params.label: Statistic of each period
params.help: The statistic taken over the observations of each period (the fold the trend is fit to); the mean is FORCE's usual choice.

params.label: Period
labels: Day of the year (of every year)
params.help: The periods the statistic is folded into, and so the steps of the trend: every year (the slope is per year), or the same quarter, month, week or day of the year across all the years (the slope is per quarter, month...). Periods without a value are skipped by the fit but still count as steps.

params.label: Confidence level
params.help: Confidence level of the t-test of the slope (0.95: significance level 0.05).

params.label: Test
labels: Decrease only (is the slope significantly negative?)
Increase only (is the slope significantly positive?)
params.help: The tail of the test of the slope: with one tail only a slope on that side can be significant (the significance is -1 for a decrease, 1 for an increase, 0 otherwise).

params.label: Weigh a drop by its recovery (FORCE's CHANGE_PENALTY)
params.help: Weight each loss by what the series has lost by the next period with a value (the loss times the value before it less the next value, over 10000), which discounts a dip the series recovers from. A loss with no period with a value after it is not considered. The change written is the unweighted one of the loss chosen.

params.label: Statistics
labels: Time of the change (the year, or the period's number)
Offset (fit at the first period), whole series
Gain (% of the offset), whole series
Periods with a value, whole series
Offset (fit at the first period), before the change
Gain (% of the offset), before the change
Periods with a value, before the change
Offset (fit at the first period), after the change
Gain (% of the offset), after the change
Periods with a value, after the change
params.help: The statistics to write, a map each: the change (the previous value less the one at the change: positive for a loss), the loss (as a percentage of the whole fold's offset), the time of the change (the year when folded by year, else the number of the quarter, month, week or day), and the twelve statistics of the linear trend for the whole fold, the part before the change and the part from it on (a part with fewer than 3 periods with a value has only its mean and counts).

tools.name: Clear-sky observations (FORCE CSO)
tools.description: FORCE's clear-sky observations (TSA CSO, Frantz 2019), as zeit.clear_observations: how many valid observations each pixel has in windows of months, and the gaps between them. The windows begin on the first day of the month of the first date and go on, `months` months each, until the one that holds the last date, which is kept whole (FORCE leaves out a last window that starts in the month of its range's end; here every window is made). An observation is valid where its value is not missing (clouds, the quality band and NoData are missing). In each window the gaps, in days, are: from the start of the window to the first valid observation, between consecutive valid observations, and from the last one to the end of the window; observations on the same day make no gap; a window without a valid observation has one gap, as long as the window, and a count of 0. A raster run writes, for each chosen statistic, one band per window, labelled with its first month (YYYY-MM); a pixel run lists the windows. The series needs real dates in order.

params.label: Window
params.help: The length of each window, in months (1 to 12). The windows are calendar months, from the first day of the first date's month.

params.label: Statistics
params.help: Clear observations is the number of valid observations in the window; the others are statistics of the gaps in days between them (the longest gap is the maximum, the mean revisit time the mean). Unlike FORCE, which divides some of them by the number of observations instead of the number of gaps, every statistic but the count is that of the same gaps.

tools.name: Polar phenology (FORCE)
tools.description: FORCE's polar land surface phenology (TSA POL, Frantz's polar-hl.c after Brooks et al. 2020), as zeit.polar_metrics. The series is put on a circle (the day of the year the angle, the value the radius, negative values counted as 0); the mean of all its points is the long-term mean vector, its opposite, the time of least activity, starts the phenological year. Each year's season runs from that start to the next; the values are accumulated along it and divided by its total, and the dates where the fraction reaches the start, middle and end thresholds are the start, middle and end of the season. Then the early and late minima, the peak, the mean vectors, amplitudes, integrals and rates of rise and fall. The series must be regular, a constant step of whole days over at least 2 calendar years, a non-negative index: run Interpolate (regular grid) first and run Polar phenology on its result. A missing step is filled by linear interpolation in time. A raster run writes, for each chosen metric, one band per calendar year, labelled with it; a season belongs to the year it ends in, so the first or the last year may be empty. The date metrics (D*) are days since 1 January of the band's year, in a calendar of 365 days (29 February shares day 60 with 1 March); the other metrics are in the unit of the data (integrals: times a year or a month; rates: per month). A pixel run lists the metrics by year and marks the date metrics on the chart.

params.label: Metrics
labels: DEM: date of the early minimum (days)
DLM: date of the late minimum (days)
DSS: date of the start of the season (days)
DMS: date of the middle of the season (days)
DES: date of the end of the season (days)
DEV: date of the mean vector of the early growing season (days)
DAV: date of the mean vector of the growing season (days)
DLV: date of the mean vector of the late growing season (days)
LTS: length of the total season (days)
LGS: length of the growing season (days)
LGV: length between the early and late mean vectors (days)
VEM: value at the early minimum
VLM: value at the late minimum
VSS: value at the start of the season
VMS: value at the middle of the season
VES: value at the end of the season
VEV: length of the early mean vector
VAV: length of the growing season's mean vector
VLV: length of the late mean vector
VGM: mean value of the growing season
VGV: standard deviation of the growing season
DPY: start of the phenological year (days)
DPV: shift of the season's start from DPY (days)
params.help: The polar metrics to write, one map series each; only what they need is computed. D*: dates in days since 1 January of the band's year; L*: lengths in days; V*: values in the unit of the data; I*: integrals; R*: rates.

params.label: Start of the season
params.help: The fraction of the season's accumulated value that marks its start (FORCE's POL_START_THRESHOLD, 0.2).

params.label: Middle of the season
params.help: The fraction that marks the middle of the season (POL_MID_THRESHOLD, 0.5).

params.label: End of the season
params.help: The fraction that marks the end of the season (POL_END_THRESHOLD, 0.8).

params.label: Each season's own mean vector moves its start
params.help: Fine-tune the start of each year's season from its own mean vector (FORCE's POL_ADAPTIVE). Without it the shift (DPV) is 0.

tools.name: Tasseled Cap (FORCE)
tools.description: Tasseled Cap brightness, greenness and wetness (Zeit's zeit.tasseled_cap, FORCE's TC-BRIGHT, TC-GREEN, TC-WET and TC-DI): each component is a fixed weighted sum of the six reflective bands (blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2) of a date, in float32 with FORCE's order of operations, so that its values truncated to integers are FORCE's. Brightness is soil and built-up, greenness green vegetation, wetness moisture and shade; the disturbance is brightness - greenness - wetness of the same matrix (FORCE's TC-DI, not the standardized index of Healey et al. 2005). Needs Landsat-style surface reflectance (map the six bands) with real dates; Sentinel-2's NIR for FORCE is B8A, so map B8A to NIR. A raster run writes one series per component and opens each as a new layer, ready for LandTrendr, BFAST and the other tools.

params.label: Components
params.help: What to compute, one series each. The disturbance is brightness - greenness - wetness of the matrix used, as it comes.

params.label: Coefficients
labels: Each date's sensor (TM Crist, ETM+ Huang 2002, OLI Baig 2014, MSI Crist)
params.help: Crist (1985, RSE 17:301-306), derived for Landsat 4-5 TM reflectance factors, is the matrix FORCE applies to every sensor. Each date's sensor: the matrix published for it (Landsat 4-5 Crist 1985, Landsat 7 ETM+ Huang et al. 2002, Landsat 8-9 OLI Baig et al. 2014, Sentinel-2 Crist 1985 as FORCE), with the sensor read from the scene each date came from (its STAC platform, else its file name: LC08_..., LE07_..., S2B_...); a date of another sensor is an error. Huang et al. (2002, IJRS 23:1741-1748) and Baig et al. (2014, Remote Sensing Letters 5:423-431) were derived for at-satellite (top-of-atmosphere) reflectance: applying them to surface reflectance is common practice but approximate, and only Crist's matrix was derived for surface reflectance factors.

params.label: Reflectance units
params.help: The bands are taken as reflectance x 10000 (the scale of FORCE's integers, and of Zeit's Landsat tools in Janus), and the result is in it. Automatic: median <= 2 -> reflectance 0-1; median >= 6500 -> Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 digital numbers (x 0.0000275 - 0.2); otherwise already x 10000. Janus applies the files' scale/offset metadata first, when present.

tools.name: Spectral adjustment to Sentinel-2A (FORCE)
tools.description: Landsat or MODIS surface reflectance on the spectral response of Sentinel-2A, with the red edge bands and the broad NIR those sensors do not have predicted (Zeit's zeit.spectral_adjust: FORCE's spectral adjustment, Scheffler, Frantz and Segl 2020, RSE 241:111723). Each sensor (Landsat 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, MODIS Terra, MODIS Aqua) has 50 clusters of spectra and a global one, each with a regression of the ten Sentinel-2A bands on its six (blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2); each pixel's prediction is the average of the regressions of the closest clusters by spectral angle. All ten bands are rewritten, not only the new ones. Needs Landsat-style surface reflectance (map the six bands) with real dates. The ten bands are written as series, one layer each (reflectance x 10000). Dates of Sentinel-2 are refused (Zeit passes them through with their ten bands, which Janus does not map).

params.label: Sensor
params.help: The sensor of every date. Each date's own: read from the scene the date came from (its STAC platform, else its file name: LC08_..., LT05_..., MOD09...); a date whose sensor is not found is an error, and so is a Sentinel-2 one. For MODIS, map SWIR1 to band 6 and SWIR2 to band 7.

params.label: Reflectance units
params.help: The bands are taken as reflectance x 10000 (the scale of FORCE's integers, and of Zeit's Landsat tools in Janus), and the result is in it. Automatic: median <= 2 -> reflectance 0-1; median >= 6500 -> Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 digital numbers (x 0.0000275 - 0.2); otherwise already x 10000. Janus applies the files' scale/offset metadata first, when present.

params.label: FORCE's first cluster search (skips cluster 9)
params.help: FORCE's first search for the closest cluster skips cluster 9 (it tests s != 9 where it means to leave out the global cluster, as its other searches do) and lets the global cluster be the first pick. On: the search as FORCE has it, so that the values truncated to integers are FORCE's in every pixel. Off: the search as the paper means it (cluster 9 competes, the global cluster is never the first pick), which differs from FORCE's integers by more than 1 in 1.6-2.3% of the observations of synthetic mixtures.

tools.name: NBAR (c-factor)
tools.description: Nadir BRDF-adjusted reflectance (Zeit's zeit.nbar: the c-factor method of Roy et al. 2016 and 2017, as in FORCE and HLS): each band is multiplied by the ratio of the Ross-Thick / Li-Sparse-Reciprocal model of MODIS (three fixed parameters per band) at nadir view and a normalized solar zenith to the model at the pixel's own sun and view angles, so that dates seen under different sun and view geometries become comparable. Map the bands to normalize (any of coastal, blue, green, red, red edge 1-3, NIR (Sentinel-2's B08), NIR narrow (B8A, OLI's band 5), SWIR1, SWIR2; at least one) and, unless the angles come from Sentinel-2's metadata, the four angle bands of each date (sza, saa, vza, vaa: solar and view zenith and azimuth, e.g. Landsat Collection 2's SZA, SAA, VZA and VAA bands, or angle rasters stacked with the bands). For Sentinel-2 the angles can instead be read from each date's granule metadata (MTD_TL.xml: the 5 km grids of ESA, interpolated to the pixels as Zeit's zeit.sentinel2_angles does, with the view angles of one band for all, B06 as HLS), found in the STAC items the series was made from or beside the Sentinel-2 product's files. Reflectance, not digital numbers with an offset; the result is in the units of the input. A pixel with a zenith outside 0-90 degrees or an angle without a value is missing. Not for snow (the parameters are MODIS's snow-free ones), and not for HLS, which is already NBAR. A raster run writes one series per band (and per c-factor, if asked) and opens each as a new layer.

params.label: Sun and view angles from
labels: The four angle bands of each date (sza, saa, vza, vaa)
params.help: Where the angles of each pixel come from. The angle bands: four bands of each date's file, mapped by role (Landsat Collection 2, HLS). Sentinel-2 granule metadata: ESA's 5 km grids of the tile (the sun's zenith and azimuth, the view zenith and azimuth of each band and detector) read from each date's MTD_TL.xml, the detectors of a band fused, interpolated bilinearly to the pixels (Roy et al. 2017) as Zeit's zeit.sentinel2_angles does; the files are found from the STAC items the series was made from (its VRTs record them) or from the Sentinel-2 product a date's file is in (.SAFE/GRANULE/.../MTD_TL.xml, or an MTD_TL.xml beside the file); a date without metadata stops the run. The angle bands are then not needed and the unit parameter is not used (the grids are in degrees).

params.label: Sentinel-2 view band
params.help: Only with the angles from Sentinel-2's metadata: the band whose view zenith and azimuth every band takes. B06 (the second red edge band) is HLS's choice (User Guide, Sec. 6.3): one view geometry for all bands, the detectors' offsets between bands being up to a fraction of a degree.

params.label: Normalized solar zenith
labels: Each date's scene mean (Roy et al. 2016, 2017)
params.help: The solar zenith the reflectance is brought to (the view is always nadir). Scene mean: the mean of the observed solar zenith of each date over the pixels of the run's window whose four angles are valid, as Zeit does (the window, not the whole image: change it and the means change). On the chart there is no scene, so a pixel's own solar zenith is used and its dates are only brought to nadir. Roy et al. (2016) advise against a normalized zenith far from the observed ones.

params.label: Fixed solar zenith (degrees)
params.help: The solar zenith every date is brought to when the normalized zenith is a fixed angle (0 to 90 degrees).

params.label: Angle bands' unit
labels: Hundredths of a degree (Landsat Collection 2, HLS)
params.help: Only with the angles from bands. The unit of the four angle bands. Landsat Collection 2's SZA, SAA, VZA and VAA bands and HLS's store hundredths of a degree (integers; 3025 is 30.25 degrees); angles from Sentinel-2's tile metadata are in degrees. With hundredths read as degrees every pixel is missing (zeniths of thousands of degrees); with degrees read as hundredths the angles are nearly zero and the result is wrong without a warning.

params.label: Also write the c-factors
params.help: A series of the c-factor (NBAR over observed reflectance; not clipped, within 0.95-1.05 in a Landsat's field of view) of each band, to inspect the correction.

tools.name: ImproPhe (FORCE)
tools.description: Sharpens a coarse series to the pixels of this finer one, as zeit.improphe (FORCE's CF- and L2-ImproPhe; Frantz et al. 2016, IEEE TGRS 54:4153-4164): each pixel's value is the weighted mean of the coarse values at the pixels of its neighbourhood that look like it in the fine data (the fine scenes averaged in seasonal windows of the year, reduced to principal components and standardized), weighted by the spectral difference, the fine texture and the coarse texture. Two uses. A continuous field of the coarse series with one layer a year (a 500 m phenology metric of each year, say) is sharpened with the fine scenes of that year (CF-ImproPhe); the scenes of a coarser sensor (Landsat at 30 m) are sharpened with all the fine scenes of the series (Sentinel-2 at 10 m; L2-ImproPhe). The coarse series is another open series, in the same CRS, picked below; this series (all its bands of each date, its quality band applied) is the fine one, and the output is on its grid and window, a band for each layer of the coarse series (each band of it) with the coarse series' dates. The whole window is held in memory and the cost grows with the area of the neighbourhood circle: choose the ROI, or the visible area, and a kernel size that fits.

params.label: Coarse series
params.help: The series to sharpen: another open series (File > Open) in the same CRS as this one, on any grid (nearest neighbour onto this one's, as FORCE's read does). One band a date is a single field; several bands a date are several fields (the phenology metrics of one year, the bands of a Landsat scene), each sharpened. Dates with no value, and its NoData, are missing: those pixels come out empty and are not neighbours.

params.label: The coarse series is
labels: A field with a layer a year (CF-ImproPhe)
params.help: A field with a layer for each year (the dates' years must be different) is sharpened year by year with the fine scenes of that year. Scenes of a coarser sensor are each sharpened with the seasonal means of all the fine dates. Detected: scenes if some year has several dates; a series with one date a year is asked about (it could be either).

params.label: Seasonal windows
params.help: The limits of the seasonal windows in days of the year (FORCE's SEASONAL_WINDOW), n + 1 integers for n windows, in FORCE's 365-day calendar (29 February is day 60, with 1 March). A limit larger than the next one makes a window that crosses the new year (330,60,330). A window without a scene at a pixel takes the mean of all the scenes.

params.label: Kernel radius
params.help: The radius of the circle whose pixels are the neighbours, in the series' map units (FORCE's KERNEL_SIZE), turned into fine pixels by truncation: it should be a multiple of the pixel size. 2500 is 250 pixels of 10 m, minutes for a 1000 x 1000 window: the cost grows with the circle's area, so try a smaller radius (300-500) on a preview first. Pixels within the radius of the window's edge see fewer neighbours.

params.label: Texture radius
params.help: The radius of the window of the texture (the largest standard deviation of the components, and the coarse values' own), in map units (FORCE's KERNEL_TEXT), truncated to fine pixels.

params.label: Variance kept by the components
params.help: The fraction of the variance of the seasonal means the principal components keep (FORCE: 0.975).

params.label: FORCE's arithmetic
params.help: Off: the method as the paper describes it (float seasonal means, the last window including day 365, the principal components). On: FORCE's to the letter, to reproduce its output: the means cut to integers (right only for reflectance times 10000), the upper limit of every window excluded (day 365 is in none of the default seasons), and FORCE's components.

params.label: Components
params.help: The components whose distances choose the neighbours. FORCE's projects the data on the rows of the eigenvector matrix, a rotation that is not the principal axes; neither is better throughout on the synthetic data Zeit compared.

tools.name: Level 1C to surface reflectance (FORCE)
tools.description: Sentinel-2 Level 1C to surface reflectance, as zeit.level2: FORCE's force-l2ps (Frantz 2019, Remote Sensing 11:1124; FORCE by David Frantz), run in the Zeit core. The scene's top-of-atmosphere reflectance is corrected for the gases and the water vapour, the aerosols (the optical depth estimated from dark targets), the adjacency effect, the topography (with a digital elevation model) and the BRDF, and written on the scene's 10 m grid: the bottom-of-atmosphere reflectance (10 bands, blue to SWIR 2, times 10000, as int16, -9999 where there is no data), the quality information (QAI: clouds, shadows, snow, water, ...), and the distance to the clouds, the view zenith, the haze optimized transform, the aerosol optical depth and the water vapour. The cloud, shadow, snow and water flags are those of Zeit's Fmask 4.7 (Qiu, Zhu and Woodcock 2019, Remote Sensing of Environment 231:111205). Choose a .SAFE folder of a Level 1C product (JPEG 2000 or GeoTIFF bands), or a folder holding .SAFE folders: each is processed in turn, in the order of its name, never two at once. The results go to the output folder, a subfolder named after each product with boa.tif, qai.tif, dst.tif, vzn.tif, hot.tif, aod.tif and wvp.tif and attrs.json (the scene's date, sensor, aerosol, water vapour and Fmask summary); the surface reflectance and the quality information open as layers. Sentinel-2 L1C only. A scene needs about 13 GiB of memory (18 GiB with the merge of the 20 m bands), measured on a whole 110 km tile, and takes minutes: close what you can before a run, and it cannot be stopped within a scene, only between scenes.

params.label: Level 1C folder
params.help: A .SAFE folder of a Sentinel-2 Level 1C product, or a folder that holds .SAFE folders (each is processed in turn, sorted by name, one at a time).

params.label: Digital elevation model
params.help: A raster of elevations in metres, of any grid and CRS (the Copernicus GLO-30, SRTM...): put on the scene's 10 m grid by bilinear resampling. Needed by the topographic correction, and used by the Fmask.

params.label: Merge the 20 m bands
labels: No (the 20 m bands as they are, on the 10 m grid)
params.help: Predict the six 20 m bands (red edge 1-3, NIR, SWIR 1 and 2) at 10 m from the 10 m bands, on the top-of-atmosphere reflectance and before the correction, as force-l2ps does. It needs about a third more memory.

params.label: BRDF correction
params.help: Normalize the reflectance to nadir view and the scene's own sun (FORCE's DO_BRDF).

params.label: Topographic correction
params.help: Correct the illumination of the relief (FORCE's DO_TOPO); it needs the digital elevation model.

params.label: Estimate the aerosols
params.help: Estimate the aerosol optical depth from the dark targets of the scene (FORCE's DO_AOD). Off: a fixed fallback spectrum.

params.label: Adjacency effect
params.help: Correct the light scattered from the neighbouring pixels (FORCE's DO_ENV).

params.label: Multiple scattering
params.help: Include the multiple scattering of the atmosphere in the radiative transfer (FORCE's MULTI_SCATTERING).

params.label: Erase the clouds
params.help: Write no data where the Fmask finds opaque cloud (FORCE's ERASE_CLOUDS).

params.label: Fmask for the flags
params.help: Run Zeit's Fmask 4.7 for the cloud, shadow, snow and water flags. Off: no cloud detection, the QAI has no such flags.

params.label: Fmask as FORCE's baseline
params.help: Zeit's compatibility switch of the Fmask (as zeit.level2's fmask_compat).

params.label: Global Surface Water Occurrence (optional)
params.help: A raster of the water occurrence (JRC's GSWO, in percent), used by the Fmask for the water flags; none: the Fmask's own.

tools.name: EOF / principal components
tools.description: The temporal empirical orthogonal functions (EOF, principal components) of the window, as zeit.eof: the few maps (EOFs) and the time series (principal components, PCs) that explain most of its variability. The seasonal cycle is taken out of each pixel first (anomalies), the pixels are weighted by the area they cover, and the cube (dates by pixels) is decomposed from its small side, the dates: exactly (the Gram matrix of the dates) or by a randomized range finder with power iterations (Halko, Martinsson and Tropp 2011) in a few passes over the pixels, so a window that does not fit in memory works (its anomalies are kept as float32 in memory, or in a scratch file of the run's folder when they would take more than a quarter of the RAM). Each mode's map is in data units per standard deviation of its PC (or orthonormal), with its share of the variance and North's test (North et al. 1982) of whether it is separable from its neighbours; the PCs of the dates with too few valid pixels come from the gappy projection of Everson and Sirovich (1995). The first modes can be rotated by Kaiser's (1958) varimax to patterns that are more local. A raster run writes the maps of the first modes (each with its PC as the amplitude, shown with its variance), pcs.csv and eof.json in the run's folder. The decomposition needs the whole window: raster runs only.

params.label: Modes computed
params.help: How many modes are computed (at most the number of dates minus one). North's test and the rotation use them.

params.label: Maps written
params.help: How many of the first modes are written as maps (each a layer with its PC).

params.label: Anomalies
params.help: What is taken out of each pixel's series: the calendar months' means (the climatology; a month needs two values at least), a constant and sine and cosine pairs of the year fitted by least squares, or only the mean. The EOFs are of what is left.

params.label: Harmonics
params.help: The sine and cosine pairs of the harmonic fit (the anomalies 'A harmonic fit').

params.label: Pixel weights
params.help: Area: each pixel counts for what it covers (its geodesic area in the series' CRS), normalized to mean 1; cosine of the latitude is for a geographic CRS; none counts every pixel the same. Without a CRS the pixels count the same.

params.label: Maps in
labels: Data units per standard deviation of the PC
params.help: Units: each EOF in the data's units per standard deviation of its PC (the PCs have unit variance). Orthonormal: unit-length maps, the PCs carry the variance.

params.label: Solver
params.help: Automatic: exact with up to 256 dates (one pass over the pixels), else randomized. Randomized reads the pixels a few times (power iterations + 2) and is as good as exact for the first modes.

params.label: Oversampling
params.help: The randomized solver's extra columns beyond the modes computed.

params.label: Power iterations
params.help: The randomized solver's passes that sharpen the range; more passes are exacter and read the pixels again.

params.label: Rotate the first modes
params.help: Rotate this many of the first modes by Kaiser's varimax (0 for none, otherwise at least 2). The rotated maps are written too, ordered by their variance.

params.label: Kaiser normalization
params.help: Varimax with the rows divided by their communality (Kaiser's normalization).

params.label: North's test counts
labels: The effective dates (lag-1 autocorrelation of each PC)
params.help: The number of independent dates in the sampling error of each eigenvalue (North et al. 1982): all the dates, or T (1 - rho) / (1 + rho) with the lag-1 autocorrelation rho of each PC, fewer for a smooth series.

params.label: Valid fraction of a pixel
params.help: A pixel is kept when this fraction of the dates (after the anomalies) is valid; the others have no value in the maps.

params.label: Random seed
params.help: The seed of the randomized solver's test matrix (the result does not depend on the threads).

params.label: Correlation maps
params.help: Also write, for each map, the correlation of every pixel's anomalies with the mode's PC.

tools.name: Lagged correlation
tools.description: The correlation of every pixel's series with a driver (a climate index, a regional mean, another map series) at several lags, as zeit.lagged_correlation. At lag k the pairs are the pixel's value at t and the driver's at t - k: the driver leads, so a driver that acts two months later shows its strongest correlation at lag 2. Both series are averaged to calendar months first (a monthly index against a 16-day series) or matched by date, the seasonal cycle is taken out, and the pairs are the dates where both are valid. The significance is a two-sided Student t test with the effective number of pairs n (1 - rx ry) / (1 + rx ry) (Bretherton et al. 1999), because the consecutive values of a series are not independent; the best lag's p-value is adjusted for having tried the lags (Sidak), and the best lags of all the pixels are tested together by the false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995; Wilks 2016), written as q and as the map of the significant pixels. The driver is another open series (of any grid and CRS, put on this one's grid), the mean of that series over the window, or a CSV file of dates and values. Raster runs only.

params.label: Driver series
params.help: The driver: another open series (File > Open), on any grid and in any CRS, put on this series' grid (nearest neighbour or bilinear). Its first band of each date is used. Needed when the driver is a series or its window mean.

params.label: The driver is
labels: The series' mean over the window
params.help: Pixel by pixel: each pixel against the driver's pixel at the same place. The mean over the window: one series (a regional index) for every pixel. A CSV file: one series of dates and values (a header line is skipped).

params.label: Driver CSV
params.help: The CSV of the driver: a date (2020-03-15, or 2020-03 for a month) and a value on each line, comma, semicolon or tab separated; empty or NA values are missing.

params.label: Lags
params.help: The lags 0, 1, ..., K, in months or in dates (below). At lag k the driver is k steps before the pixel's value.

params.label: The lags are in
params.help: Months: both are averaged to calendar months first, so a monthly index and a 16-day series are compared and the lags are months. Dates: the driver is matched to the series' dates and the lags are observations of the series.

params.label: Dates are matched
labels: To the nearest date within the tolerance
To a date of the same month
To a date of the same year
params.help: For lags in dates: how the driver's dates are paired with the series' dates.

params.label: Tolerance
params.help: For the nearest date: how far apart the two dates may be.

params.label: Anomalies
params.help: Taken out of both series before correlating. The raw values correlate their trends and seasonal cycles too, which inflates r and makes the lags a matter of the season.

params.label: Correlation
params.help: Pearson's r, or Spearman's on the ranks of the pairs of each lag.

params.label: Best lag
params.help: Which lag is the best of each pixel.

params.label: Minimum pairs
params.help: A lag with fewer pairs of valid values has no correlation.

params.label: Effective number of pairs
params.help: The p-values use n (1 - rx ry) / (1 + rx ry) pairs (Bretherton et al. 1999), accounting for the autocorrelation of both series. Off takes the pairs as independent, which makes the p-values too small for smooth series.

params.label: Sidak adjustment of the best lag
params.help: The best lag's p-value is adjusted for the number of lags tried: 1 - (1 - p)^(K + 1).

params.label: False discovery rate
params.help: Of the pixels marked significant, about this fraction is expected to be false discoveries (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995). Wilks (2016) recommends twice the level a single test would have: 0.10 for 0.05.

params.label: Driver resampling
params.help: How the driver series is put on this series' grid when it is on another one.

outputs.name: Effective pairs at the best lag
